interpretation.interpretation: The diagram most likely shows the phases of the moon in relation to the sun. The right circle with radiating strokes is the sun, the left circle on the opposite side of the orbit is the full moon (or the earth/moon in opposition), and the thick horizontal line is the axis of opposition between them. The large circular line is the moon's orbit. The crescent shapes near the sun represent the waxing and waning thin crescents, the two half-discs at the top and bottom represent the first and last quarters, and the two shapes at the left, larger than half, represent the gibbous phases. The moon is thus shown at eight positions around its circuit, with the illuminated part always turned towards the sun, so that the phase grows as the moon moves away from the sun and is full when opposite it.
interpretation.evidence: The diagram has no transcribed text, so the interpretation rests on visible features. The right circle is surrounded by short radiating strokes, which is a conventional way of depicting the sun. The shapes on the circular line grow progressively from thin crescents (nearest the sun) through half-discs to larger-than-half shapes, and finally to the full circle opposite the sun. This progression matches the sequence of lunar phases. The straight line joining the two large circles marks the sun-moon alignment. Step 1 named the left circle and the right circle only by visual description and did not state their identity; Step 1 also recorded the shapes as 'connected_to' the circular line, which is a visual overlap and not a physical link. The identification relies on knowledge of medieval computus and astronomical diagrams, with no source named, so certainty is medium. The left circle could alternatively be read as the earth, but its position on the orbit suggests the full moon.
